instructions.question: How high on the six-rung strength ladder does the AI coding session described in `action` belong? The rungs are ordered by the cost of a miss and by how much later work rests on this session's result, not by whether a written procedure exists or how many lines the change spans: a listed correction pass whose miss the next independent review still catches sits in the middle even on a large, security-sensitive codebase; the first review or first live run whose verdicts or effects everything after it inherits sits at the top even when its steps are clearly written. Read four signals in the description: (1) what a miss costs, from a rework cycle, through a wrong verdict that later phases build on, to real money, real data or a live external system touched outside the run; (2) whether another gate still stands between this session and that consequence (a later independent review, offline tests, a sandbox) or this session is itself the last gate; (3) whether the object is new and unverified (the first review of a new system; the first review of a large change that adds new components, provider products or a guard whose scope later work relies on; the first live run of new code) or a repeat pass over something already reviewed once (a correction pass against named findings, or the review of such a pass); (4) whether one reader can hold the whole object, or the risk is that any single reader misses something, so that only many independent readers cross-checking one another would do.
instructions.tradeoff: Each rung costs more tokens and time than the one below and buys less per step. Independent index measurements give the lower-cost model 42, 51, 54, 56 and 58 points at $0.55, $1.34, $1.82, $3.46 and $5.98 per task across the five single-session rungs, and the most capable model 47, 49, 51, 53 and 53 at $2.37, $2.98, $3.91, $5.98 and $7.63; the sixth rung multiplies the cost again by the number of agents. Above high the general-benchmark gain per rung is 0 to 2 points, so the upper rungs are earned by stakes and dependence, not by size, and a rung too high wastes a multiple of the cost while a rung too low risks the miss the ladder exists to prevent.

criteria: low: the cheapest rung, for work whose miss costs almost nothing and on which nothing later rests: recording given answers, relaying a message, running a named command, a subagent's mechanical step. Measured on an independent index, the lower-cost model scores 42 at $0.55 per task here against 51 at $1.34 one rung up, and the most capable model 47 at $2.37 against 49 at $2.98; the first token arrives in about 6 seconds on both. On a code-review benchmark the most capable model at this rung found 61.0% of 105 known issues in 18 minutes 38 seconds per review, more than it found at high (57.1% in 21 minutes 36 seconds), but on an abstract-reasoning set the lower-cost model loses 17 points against the next rung (70.1% against 87.5%), so the rung is for work that needs no reasoning, not for cheap reasoning.

medium: a bounded, documented change inside a clear procedure, where a miss is caught by the existing tests or the next reviewer and little rests on this session alone: a fix whose file and defect are already named, with a test; filling a template; summarising results; a small edit. The lower-cost model defaults here: index 51 at $1.34 per task (2.4 times low for +9 points), 97.5% and 87.5% on the two abstract-reasoning sets. On a seeded-defect review its high rung found no more than this one (6.50 against 6.58 of 13 items) for 1.4 times the cost, and in a hands-on coding run high bought nothing over medium at $0.16 per task and 20 seconds median. On a repository coding benchmark the most capable model's score peaks at this rung because its higher rungs add unrequested changes outside the task.

high: real judgement with moderate stakes, where a miss costs a rework cycle but a later independent review or gate still stands between this session and merge: reviewing a bounded diff for defects, a correction pass that fixes named findings each with a test, diagnosing a failing check, drafting a plan section. The most capable model defaults here (index 51 at $3.91 per task). The lower-cost model reaches 54 at $1.82 (1.36 times medium for +3) and posts its best abstract-reasoning scores at this rung (98.5% and 93.3%, above its own extra high and max). In a controlled benchmark at this rung one lower-cost session delivered 4 of 4 tickets with 0 regressions on a 35,000-line project for $6.15 in 24 minutes and scored 24 to 25 of 25 in blind review. One published practitioner policy runs implementers at medium and reviewers of shipping code at the next rung.

extra high: complex judgement where a miss reaches the merge or misleads the next session: designing a multi-part change, reconciling conflicting rules, the exact-head review that gates a merge of an already-reviewed component, a correction pass across a large harness with many findings, verifying a large piece of work whose soundness is already partly established. Cost roughly doubles over high: the lower-cost model scores 56 at $3.46 (1.9 times high for +2 points, about 66,000 output tokens per task, first token after 144 seconds instead of 39), the most capable 53 at $5.98 (1.53 times high for +2, first token after 118 seconds). On a seeded-defect review this rung found 0.9 more of 13 defects than high at 2.2 times the cost on the lower-cost model, and 0.66 more on the most capable; work-task ratings rose about 130 and 100 Elo over high. In one week-long practitioner test the most capable model at this rung handed off much of the work to subagents; on either model the first token of a hard request arrives after about two minutes.

max: the deepest single-session reasoning, for work where a miss is expensive or irreversible and later work rests on the result: the first independent review of a large new system, or of a large change that adds new architecture, new components, new provider products or a new guard whose scope later work relies on, whose verdicts the next phases build on; the first live run of new code against an external provider with a real secret, where a wrong call costs money or touches data outside the run; root-cause analysis after earlier fixes failed; an audit for any way to bypass a new guard. Independent measurements say it buys little on average: the lower-cost model gains +2 index points over extra high (58 at $5.98, 1.73 times the cost, about 119,000 output tokens per task against 66,000), +42 and +26 Elo on work tasks, +1.9 points on scientific coding, nothing on terminal tasks and 0.8 less on abstract reasoning; the most capable model gains 0 index points (53 at $7.63, 1.28 times the cost, 1.58 times the tokens, first token after 233 seconds), +1.0 and 0 on the two abstract-reasoning sets and +9 and +14 Elo on work tasks, and on a seeded-defect review it found no more than at extra high for 1.9 times the cost. Where it helped: on 13 hard review cases a higher-effort pipeline configuration caught 10 against 8 for the lower-effort one, at 14% more tokens, with precision falling from 66.7% to 52.0% and one fewer of 80 ordinary cases caught; one published practitioner policy reserves it for auth, crypto, secrets, money, deploys, deletion and migration, the classes where a missed bug is costly and rare. A full evaluation run at this rung took 72 to 76 minutes and $22 to $29 per test, and one hard prompt on the lower-cost model exhausted a 128,000-token budget twice while still reasoning.

ultracode: the top rung, a strength level above max: many independent agents each examining or cross-checking part of the work, for work where one reader missing something is the main risk and the result must hold for everything that follows: a codebase-wide sweep of every service for one class of defect before a public launch, a first live run against real money or real accounts where every path must be independently verified, the first review of a very large new system with many independent verdict surfaces. In the coding harness it is the many-agent workflow setting: every request runs at extra high and the session orchestrates a dynamic workflow of agents, documented at up to 16 concurrent and 1,000 per run with no token cap. No measured run of this setting exists for either model; the case for it rests on independence measured on older models: reviewer agents with error correlation of 0.05 to 0.25 lifted bug detection from 32.8% for one agent to 72.4% combined and 79.3% for the best pair, at a 50% false-positive rate; a second model reviewing another's drafts raised pass rate from 71.6% to 89.7% while self-review gained nothing; aggregating ten reviews raised recall 118%. Costs multiply: ten parallel agents use quota ten times faster, a 5-agent system used 41 times the tokens of one agent, one 5-agent pre-check used 471,480 tokens in 264 seconds, and a managed many-agent review averages about 20 minutes and $15 to $25 per review. In a controlled benchmark on a 35,000-line project, orchestration neither helped nor hurt the lower-cost model; a research synthesis puts the plateau at about four agents, and at equal compute single-agent systems matched or beat multi-agent ones on reasoning tasks; so this rung is for scale or independence a single reader cannot supply, not for a bounded diff or a listed correction.

instructions.question: Which model should run the AI coding session described in `action`, at whatever rung it needs?
instructions.tradeoff: Both are frontier agentic coding models with the same five single-session rungs; the many-agent setting is documented for any model with an extra-high rung, though the one guide that lists supported models names the lower-cost model and not the most capable one. List prices: the most capable model $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens; the strong lower-cost model $4 and $20, so 2.5 times the price per token, with cached input reads nearly equal ($0.25 against $0.20). Independent index by rung: lower-cost 42, 51, 54, 56, 58 at $0.55, $1.34, $1.82, $3.46, $5.98 per task; most capable 47, 49, 51, 53, 53 at $2.37, $2.98, $3.91, $5.98, $7.63; so the lower-cost model at high (54, $1.82) outscores the most capable at max (53, $7.63) at a quarter of the cost, and the most capable leads only at the lowest rung (47 against 42; 1450 against 1224 Elo on work tasks). Speed: the lower-cost model generates 79 to 88 tokens per second against 56 to 68; in a 179-task coding benchmark (effort unstated, harness versions differed) it cost $116 against $672 with a median of 2.2 against 7.2 minutes per task, but passed 68.7% against 87.2% of functional tests with 51 confirmed memorisation shortcuts against 17, and wrote secure code in 33.5% against 37.4% of tasks. On 200 coding trajectories (effort unstated) the lower-cost model passed 68% against 49% overall with equal pass@1 (60.7 against 61.5). Full evaluation suites at max: 69.69% at $22.30 and 72 minutes per test against 68.83% at $28.92 and 76 minutes, within error of each other; the most capable model is first on a live-coding benchmark (90.52%) and on an agent leaderboard (13.80% net improvement at $3.72 per task) on neither of which the lower-cost model has an entry yet. In a controlled orchestration benchmark at high, the most capable model as orchestrator cost 1.9 to 3.0 times more for the same 4 of 4 tickets on a 35,000-line project and scored lower in blind review (19 to 20 against 24 to 25 of 25 for the lower-cost model solo); in the same benchmark's defect review it found 4 of 5 seeded bugs for $3.79 against 3 of 5 plus one real bug for $1.25; an independent evaluator calls the lower-cost model an incremental improvement over the most capable one. Both fall back to an older model when a cyber classifier blocks a request; source-code vulnerability review runs on both. On subscription plans the most capable model draws on a 50% cap of weekly limits, and one reported five-subagent fan-out at high emptied a five-hour window in 16 minutes.

most_capable_model.what: Work where even a strong model often falls short and a miss is costly or would pass unnoticed: demanding reasoning; long autonomous work with several dependent phases; open-ended diagnosis where the cause is not yet known; designing and building a new system with many interacting parts; the first independent review of a large new system, or of a large change that adds new architecture, new components, new provider products or a new guard whose scope later work relies on, whose verdicts the next phases build on; the first run of new code against a live external service with a real secret; or work on which the lower-cost model at a higher rung has already fallen short.
most_capable_model.not_for: Work whose task list is already written and on which both models largely succeed: applying named fixes, reviewing a correction pass against the findings it claims to fix, checking results against a list, recording decisions or updating documents, even when the code is large or security-sensitive; there the 2.5 times price and the 1.6 to 3 times slower turns buy little, and on an independent index the lower-cost model at high already outscores this one at max.
examples: Find why a background job intermittently loses data after two earlier fixes failed
Build a new payment integration and run it against the provider's sandbox for the first time
First security review of a new 10,000-line service that later phases will build on

strong_lower_cost_model.what: Well-specified agentic coding, code review and knowledge work that a strong model completes reliably, including long-running coding sessions on a known task list: applying named fixes each with a test, reviewing a correction pass against the findings it claims to fix, a repeat review of a component already reviewed once, checking results against a list, recording decisions, writing or updating documents. Independent measurements put it first on general, work-task and terminal indexes at a quarter to a sixth of the cost per task, 2 to 3 times faster per task.
strong_lower_cost_model.not_for: Open-ended diagnosis or design, the first review of a large new system or of a large change that adds new components, products or guards whose verdicts others build on, long work with several dependent phases that includes a first live run of new code, or work on which this model at a higher rung has already fallen short; it also passes fewer functional tests on unseen tasks and takes memorisation shortcuts more often.
examples: Fix five review findings that each name a file and a defect, adding a test for each
Review a correction pass against the findings it says it fixed
Update the project's handoff notes after a verified release
